facts.value: 38-page Annual Treasury Management Strategy and Annual Non-Treasury Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Annex 3, doc 16001) taken from Audit and Governance Committee on 28 January 2026 to Full Council on 26 February 2026 as Agenda Item 4(3). Covering report signed off by Cllr Bill O'Donovan, Chair of the Audit and Governance Committee. Adviser: Arlingclose. Structure: covering report (paras 1-3), Appendix 1 Treasury Management Strategy (sections 1-7 including inline Appendix A Arlingclose forecast 22 Dec 2025 and inline Appendix B existing position), Appendix 2 Non-Treasury Investment Strategy (property, service loans, proportionality), Appendix 3 MRP Statement (labelled '2025-26' in the header -- carry-over typo, this is the 2026-27 approval). Read in full from local PDF. Companion Q4 2025/26 outturn (doc 16531, Audit and Governance Committee 30 July 2026) opened for officer contact and for the year-end actuals against which the strategy's forward numbers are checked.

source.title: Annual Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Annex 3) -- Council, 26 February 2026

facts.note: The strategy paper itself does not carry an officer contact block -- consistent with PIPELINE's observation that strategy appendices generally do not. The Q4 outturn (doc 16531 p.3) does: Peter Vickers (Executive Head of Finance and Section 151 Officer) and Nikki Fleming (Financial Governance Manager, report author). Both taken verbatim.

facts.value: TWO READINGS -- report both. (1) At the strategy paper's stated Appendix B date of 31/12/2025: our file returns 9 PWLB loans / £95,000,000 principal / weighted 4.7042%. Paper Appendix B PWLB row is £127.0m at 4.8%. DOES NOT TIE at that stated date -- £32m gap. (2) At the council's own year-end (31/3/2026): our file returns 11 PWLB loans / £127,000,000 principal / weighted 4.7535%. Paper's own Q4 outturn Table 2 (doc 16531) at 31.3.26 Actual: PWLB £127.0m at 4.75%. TIES EXACTLY to the pound and to two decimal places on rate. The Appendix B figures in the strategy are therefore best interpreted as year-end (31/3/2026) forecast presented in a table headed 'December 2025' -- and those numbers then became the year-end actuals. Between 31/12/2025 and 31/3/2026 the council drew about £32m of net additional PWLB (Q4 outturn Table 2 movement column shows PWLB moving from £62m at 31/3/25 to £127m at 31/3/26 = +£65m of long-term PWLB drawn in the year, offsetting a -£92m fall in short-term borrowing).

source.title: OUR file (price_book.py --as-at 2025-12-31 and 2026-03-31); paper Appendix B and Q4 outturn (doc 16531) Table 2

facts.note: Since the tie at the year-end date is exact and confirmed against the council's own subsequent outturn paper, the email can lead with the loan-book cross-check at 31/3/2026. Not framing it as a challenge to the strategy paper's date labelling.

facts.value: CHECKED AND TIES on the paper's own numbers, both forms. Form A (Loans CFR - External Borrowing = Internal Borrowing), from strategy Table 1: 24-25A 173.9-166.0=7.9; 25-26F 170.6-149.0=21.6; 26-27E 144.8-75.0=69.8; 27-28E 141.5-65.0=76.5; 28-29E 135.5-25.0=110.5 -- all tie as printed. Form B (Balance Sheet Resources - Treasury Investments/(New Borrowing) = Internal Borrowing): 24-25A 45.8-37.9=7.9; 25-26F 41.1-19.5=21.6; 26-27E 39.8-(-30.0)=69.8; 27-28E 40.3-(-36.2)=76.5; 28-29E 40.5-(-70.0)=110.5 -- all tie. On the Q4 outturn's actual year-end numbers (Table 1): 31.3.26 Loans CFR 173.8 - External borrowing 149.0 = £24.8m internal borrowing (Q4 outturn does not print an internal-borrowing figure -- this is our arithmetic on their Table 1). That is £3.2m higher than the strategy Table 1's 25-26F forecast of £21.6m for the same date.

source.title: Strategy Table 1 (Appendix 1 para 3.1, p.8); Q4 outturn Table 1 (doc 16531, Appendix 1)

facts.note: Internal borrowing came in at £24.8m actual against £21.6m forecast -- the council held slightly more internal cash / less external borrowing than the mid-year strategy expected. Not material but worth noting as a marker that the direction of travel (rising internal borrowing) is running slightly ahead of the strategy plan.

facts.value: Strategy Table 1's 2024-25 Actual column has an internal arithmetic slip: shows CFR 174.2, Less Other Debt Liabilities 0.6, then Loans CFR 173.9. But 174.2 - 0.6 = 173.6, not 173.9. Q4 outturn (doc 16531) Table 1 for the same 31.3.25 date shows Loans CFR = 173.6 (matching the arithmetic). All four forecast years (2025-26F through 2028-29E) in the strategy Table 1 tie exactly. Only the 2024-25 Actual column has the 0.3m discrepancy -- either OLL should be 0.3 or Loans CFR should be 173.6.

source.title: Strategy Table 1 vs Q4 outturn Table 1 -- 31.3.25 column

facts.value: The strategy paper explicitly plans against a ~2-year remaining life of the council under Hampshire local government reorganisation. Two direct references: (1) Appendix 1 para 4.6 -- discussing forward-starting LA-to-LA loans: 'However, the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account.' (2) Appendix 1 para 6.4 -- explaining why interest rate exposure indicator is not being set at a 1% limit: 'This is an appropriate strategy whilst interest rates are projected to be stable in the two years remaining life of the council. The Council does not consider that it is affordable to lock in current rates on a long-term basis (i.e. beyond 5 years) due to the higher rates and this would fetter the new Untary's ability to optimise its treasury strategy.' Also Appendix 1 para 5.8 (pooled funds): 'it is the councils' strategy to hold these investments for the duration of the remaning period of the council's existence.' The design of the paper follows: 1.5-year average duration on debt (para 4.4); wide-open 100% upper limits on the 12-month, 24-month and 5-year maturity bands (para 6.5); running down of external borrowing from £166.0m (24-25A) to £25.0m (28-29E); internal borrowing climbing from 4.5% of Loans CFR to 82% (7.9 -> 110.5); disinclination to lock beyond 5 years.
facts.note: This is the most distinctive feature of the reading. Of the councils read this year, none has been as explicitly framed around the timeline of the council's own existence. Handle carefully in the email -- do NOT frame as criticism, do NOT speculate on the LGR outcome; simply note the shape of the strategy and what it implies. 'Untary' is a typo for 'Unitary' in para 6.4 (also 'remaning' in para 5.8, 'Investement' in Appendix 2 title, MRP header labelled '2025-26' in a 2026-27 paper). None worth raising -- they are drafting slips, not substance.

facts.value: Q4 outturn (doc 16531) Table 2 shows a substantial rotation of the debt book during 2025/26: long-term PWLB moved from £62.0m at 31/3/25 to £127.0m at 31/3/26 (movement +£65.0m -- £65m of new long-term PWLB drawn in the year), other long-term borrowing moved £2.0m -> £12.0m (+£10.0m), and short-term borrowing dropped £102.0m -> £10.0m (-£92.0m). Total borrowing moved £166.0m -> £149.0m, a net reduction of £17.0m but with the composition fundamentally changed. Rates at 31/3/26: PWLB 4.75%, other long-term 4.58%, short-term 4.58%. Blended rate on total borrowing at 31/3/26: (127*4.75 + 12*4.58 + 10*4.58)/149 = 704.01/149 = 4.72%. Investment portfolio also changed shape: long-term investments 16.0 -> 13.0, short-term 5.0 -> 13.0, cash equivalents 18.0 -> 5.9. Net borrowing 127.0 -> 117.1.

source.title: Q4 outturn Table 2 -- Treasury Management Summary at 31.3.26

facts.note: This is direct evidence of the strategy in action -- para 4.5 of the strategy explicitly states the intention to lengthen debt duration by replacing short-term with long-term. The £65m of new long-term PWLB drawn in one year is the mechanism. Worth mentioning in the email as a concrete instance of the strategy being executed, not just described.

facts.value: Strategy Appendix 1 para 4.2: £30.0m of existing PWLB to replace in 2026/27 as loans mature; £48.0m borrowing requirement once £18m minimum-cash is included. Para 3.3: £70.0m of additional borrowing needed by 2028/29 over the forecast horizon. Table 2 liability benchmark drops from £147.5m (25-26F) to £123.0m (26-27E) to £119.2m (27-28E) to £113.0m (28-29E) -- reflecting the CFR ramp-down from £173.9m to £135.5m. Cash floor is £18m per year of which £13m is in strategic pooled funds that cannot be sold at short notice + £5m liquidity buffer (para 3.5). Financial Implications (para 7.6): interest cost budget for 2026-27 = £6.9m (ex IFRIC 4 lease interest). Investment income budget (para 7.5): £1.7m (MMF at 4% + pooled fund income). Investment income budget from Appendix 2 (para 6.2, wider than treasury only) is £10.1m against gross service expenditure of £34.2m in 2026-27 = 29.5% -- very high dependence.
facts.note: The £6.9m interest cost budget covers the short-term borrowing side. The £10.1m investment income line (Appendix 2) includes commercial property income, not just treasury. Council's revenue budget leans heavily on the property income stream (£148.2m property portfolio); if property returns weaken through the abolition transition, it lands on the general fund not the successor unitary. Internal observation, not for email.

facts.value: Strategy Appendix 1 para 5.3 -- investments at 31/12/2025: £12.8m in pooled funds (across 4 different funds); £12.2m in money market funds (next day access); £0.1m in Lloyds Bank plc (next day access); £27.0m in short-term LA investments at 'a favourable rate' returning before financial year-end. Sum: 12.8+12.2+0.1+27.0 = £52.1m -- ties para 5.2's £52.2m within rounding. Q4 outturn Table 2 at 31/3/26: long-term investments £13.0m at 4.75%, short-term investments £13.0m at 5.76%, cash and cash equivalents £5.9m at 4.07%, total investments £31.9m (down from £39.0m at 31/3/25). So the £27m LA lending had returned before year-end, as expected. Strategic pooled funds rate in Appendix B is 12.5% -- best interpreted as full-year total return including NAV recovery, not running yield (para 5.8 confirms 'Pooled fund capital values are expected to fully recover in 2026/27').

source.title: Strategy Appendix 1 paras 5.2, 5.3; Appendix B; Q4 outturn Table 2

facts.note: The £27m of LA short-term lending at 'a favourable rate' is unusually specific for a strategy paper without naming counterparties. Rushmoor is on the LENDER side of the same LA-to-LA market it also borrows from (para 4.11 says the council plans to borrow from both PWLB and other LAs). Two-way play in a market where our platform has visibility both sides.

facts.value: Appendix 2 para 4.2 property table at 31 March 2025 (£m): Industrial units cost 51.8 / value 58.0 (+6.2); Offices 36.6 / 29.6 (-7.0); Retail 42.1 / 27.3 (-14.8); Caravan Park 0.3 / 0.5 (+0.2); Petrol Stations 2.3 / 3.0 (+0.7); Waste Recycling 1.0 / 4.3 (+3.3); Mixed Use 0.2 / 0.3 (+0.1); Other 0.2 / 0.3 (+0.1); Retail & residential 24.9 / 24.9 (0). Totals: cost £159.4m, value £148.2m, aggregate impairment £(11.2)m. OUR CHECK: cost column ties to 159.4; value column ties to 148.2. Retail is down 35% from cost; Offices down 19%; Industrial up 12%. Appendix 2 s.9 -- Commercial Investments: Property forecast 148.2 (31-Mar-25A) -> 143.1 (26F) -> 126.2 (27F), i.e. planned reductions consistent with the covering report's para 3.3 note of '£31m in asset sales over the next three years, excluding the potential sale of Civic Quarter land'.

source.title: Strategy Appendix 2 para 4.2 property table; s.9 investment indicators

facts.note: The Retail impairment (-£14.8m) and Office impairment (-£7.0m) are the strain on the property book. The £31m of planned asset sales over three years, plus a potential Civic Quarter sale sitting outside, is what the debt-reduction plan (external borrowing £166m -> £25m) rests on. If sales slip or receipts come in low, the internal borrowing forecast (7.9 -> 110.5) has to absorb the difference or new external borrowing has to increase.

facts.value: Appendix A -- Arlingclose Economic and Interest Rate Forecast dated 22 December 2025. Central case: Bank Rate 3.75% current -> 3.50% Mar-26 -> 3.25% Jun-26, held at 3.25% through Dec-28 (though 'near-term upside risks to our Bank Rate forecast have increased'). 3-month money market rate 3.82% -> 3.30% mid-2026 through 2027, 3.35% by 2028. 5yr gilt 3.96% current -> 3.75% Sep-26 through mid-2028, 3.80% Dec-28. 10yr gilt 4.52% -> 4.30% Sep-26 through Dec-28. 20yr gilt 5.16% -> 4.90% mid-2026 through Dec-28. 50yr gilt 4.74% -> 4.60% Jun-26 onwards. Margins printed: PWLB Standard = gilt + 1.00%; PWLB Certainty = gilt + 0.80%; PWLB HRA = gilt + 0.40%; NWF = gilt + 0.40%. Q4 outturn (doc 16531 para 5.2) records Bank Rate still at 3.75% as at 30 July 2026 with 'a change in predictions recently from a slow reduction to maintaining this level if not having a slight increase' -- so the forecast's central-case path had already been partially disproven by the time the Q4 outturn went to committee.

source.title: Strategy Appendix A -- Arlingclose forecast 22 December 2025; Q4 outturn para 5.2 for update

facts.note: The forecast is what the strategy was set against; the Q4 outturn on the same book records that the market view has since shifted. Worth noting as a testable-and-tested-since observation. Do not tell the council the forecast was wrong -- they know; the Q4 outturn says so themselves.

facts.value: Appendix 1 s.6 -- Credit risk target: portfolio average credit rating A+ / score 5.0. Liquidity: cash available within 3 months >= £5m. Interest rate exposure (para 6.4): 'not seen as necessary to set a limit on the revenue impact of a 1% change in interest rates. The use of this indicator will be kept under review going forward' -- deferral rather than compliance with the Code's requirement. Maturity structure of borrowing (para 6.5): upper limits 100% at under-12mo, 12-24mo and 24mo-5yr bands; 0% upper at 5-10yr and 10yr+ bands; lower limits all 0%. Reported position: 53% of loans in under-12mo now, vs 91% previously. Principal Sums Invested Longer than a Year (para 6.6): 26-27 £30m / 27-28 £30m / 28-29 £20m at any one time. Counterparty limits (Table 3): UK Government unlimited to 50yr; LA/govt £10m for 25yr; MMFs £6m; secured govt-collateral £6m to 25yr; secured other-collateral £6m to 10yr; unsecured banks £3m to 13mo (sector £30m); building societies £3m to 13mo (sector £6m); strategic pooled funds £6m (sector £30m). Additional: pooled fund group £15m, broker nominee £15m, foreign country £6m (Table 4).
facts.note: The interest rate exposure indicator deferral is a candid disclosure -- but the CIPFA Treasury Management Code 2021 Edition requires the indicator to be set. Framing this as any kind of gap in the email would be picking at compliance, which we don't do. Note it for internal purposes only. The maturity structure limits at 100% upper are effectively wide-open -- consistent with the 2-year-remaining rationale, but they do not constrain refinancing risk in the conventional sense.

facts.value: Appendix 3 -- MRP Statement. Header reads 'MINIMUM REVENUE PROVISION STATEMENT 2025-26' (carry-over typo; this is the 2026-27 approval). Post-2008 capital expenditure: annuity method with annual interest rate = average relevant PWLB certainty rate for annuity loans in year of expenditure, for a term equal to asset life up to 50 years (para 5). Freehold land 50 years; capitalised non-fixed asset expenditure 20 years (para 6). Assets under finance lease or PFI: MRP = principal element of the rent/charge (para 7). Former operating leases brought on-balance-sheet under IFRS 16: MRP adjusted so overall charge reflects the right-of-use asset value on transition rather than the liability (para 8). Loans to third parties: financial-return purpose = MRP per policy of underlying assets, less loan principal repayments (para 9); service purpose = NIL MRP except for expected credit losses (para 10). Capital loans to RHL specifically: annual credit loss review + MRP on annuity basis in line with government requirements (para 13). Capex incurred during 2025/26 not subject to MRP charge until 2026/27 or later (para 15).
facts.note: MRP annuity is priced off the average relevant PWLB certainty rate for annuity loans in the year of capex -- which is a rate we publish daily. Similar shape to Tower Hamlets. Not raising this in the email for Rushmoor since the annuity-rate story does more for large HRA-holding councils; Rushmoor's MRP shape is otherwise conventional.

signals.headline: 1.5-year average debt duration at 31/12/2025 with £30m of PWLB to replace in 2026/27 (£48m borrowing requirement incl. £18m minimum cash) and 53% of loans maturing inside 12 months; £70m of additional borrowing needed by 2028/29
signals.why_it_matters: The debt book is deliberately kept short (paras 4.4-4.6) because the council will not exist in c.2 years; the successor unitary inherits the refinancing profile. The 100% upper limits across the sub-5-year bands (para 6.5) formalise this. The book has already been actively restructured -- £65m of long-term PWLB drawn in 2025/26 while £92m of short-term rolled off. Refinancing risk is high on paper but the paper explains its rationale.

signals.headline: Interest rate exposure indicator not set at a 1% revenue-impact limit -- 'not seen as necessary' (para 6.4), a deferral rather than compliance with the CIPFA Treasury Management Code 2021 Edition requirement
signals.why_it_matters: Candid disclosure that the indicator is deferred rather than compliant. The paper's own justification is that rates are 'projected to be stable in the two years remaining life of the council' and locking beyond 5 years would fetter the successor unitary. Legitimate reasoning but a Code-required indicator has not been set. Internal observation only -- not for the outreach email.

courses_named: Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members)
officer.body:
Hi Peter,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has moved since. So below are a few thoughts on Rushmoor's 2026-27 Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 26 February, read alongside the Q4 outturn that went to Audit and Governance on 30 July. You're not being singled out -- every authority gets one of these -- and there's no agenda in it. The papers are candid and carefully laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Two cross-checks first, which is where we start on any paper. Our PWLB file for Rushmoor holds eleven loans totalling £127,000,000 at a principal-weighted 4.7535%, and your Q4 outturn Table 2 at 31 March 2026 prints PWLB £127.0m at 4.75%. That ties to the pound and to two decimal places on rate, which is the strongest form the loan-book cross-check takes. Your balance-sheet identity ties on the same year-end figures too: Loans CFR £173.8m less external borrowing £149.0m leaves £24.8m of internal borrowing at 31 March 2026, £3.2m higher than the £21.6m the strategy Table 1 had forecast for the year. Nothing to raise on either side.

What's distinctive about the strategy is that it says out loud what most 2026-27 papers leave implicit. Paragraph 4.6 has "the council only has two years remaining and must take the forthcoming change into account", and paragraph 6.4 talks about not locking beyond five years because it would fetter the incoming unitary's ability to optimise its treasury strategy. Every design choice in the paper reads through that lens -- the 1.5-year average duration at 31 December, the 100% upper limits across the under-12-month, 12-to-24-month and 24-month-to-5-year bands in paragraph 6.5, the running down of external borrowing from £166.0m at 24-25 actual to £25.0m at 28-29 estimate, and internal borrowing climbing from £7.9m to £110.5m across the same forecast. Of the treasury strategies we've read this year, no other has been quite so explicitly framed around the timeline of the council's own existence. That isn't a criticism -- it's arguably the most honest way to write it -- and it makes the paper unusual to read.

The book itself did a lot of moving in 2025/26 to fit that horizon. Your Q4 outturn shows long-term PWLB going from £62.0m at 31 March 2025 to £127.0m at 31 March 2026, and short-term borrowing dropping from £102.0m to £10.0m over the same period. So around £92m of short-term rolled off and around £65m of new long-term PWLB was drawn, a net reduction of £17m across the total book but a fundamental change in shape -- and consistent with the paragraph 4.5 aim to lengthen the duration. Our monthly sector view at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity carries the timing and rates of every one of those drawings against every other council's the same month, which is useful when you're timing the next tranche of that programme against a market that has moved. Your Q4 paragraph 5.2 flags the shift since the strategy was set -- the market moving from a slow reduction path to holding or slightly increasing -- which is exactly the risk paragraph 4.5 was hedging.

What comes next is set out clearly in the strategy: £30m of PWLB to replace in 2026/27, £48m of borrowing requirement once the £18m minimum-cash floor is included, and £70m of additional borrowing needed by 2028/29 to bridge the CFR ramp down to £135.5m. The liability benchmark itself in Table 2 steps down from £147.5m at 25-26 forecast to £123.0m for 26-27 and £119.2m for 27-28 -- and paragraph 3.5 is explicit that £13m of the £18m minimum cash sits in strategic pooled funds that can't be sold at short notice, so the practical liquidity buffer is £5m. Our liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is interactive and built on live data, which is useful given that CIPFA has updates to both the Prudential and Treasury Codes coming; it puts the shape of your Table 2 alongside peer districts of similar size.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. PWLB & long-term borrowing strategy speaks to the £65m of long-term you drew this year and the £30-70m programme ahead of you; Liability benchmarking in practice covers Table 2 in more depth; Prudential Code refresh is timely given the code updates; and Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is written for the committee this goes to.
